terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation: aliquem aliquā rē spoliāre
evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.4.37: Apollōnium omnī argentō spoliāstī (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: beat up, handle roughly; Traupman’s word for “mug”
evidence: Ter. Ad. 1.2.9: ipsum dominum atque omnem familiam mulcāvit ūsque ad mortem (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Classically mulcāre is to beat, cudgel, maltreat (Plautus, Cicero); it says nothing of robbing.

terms.gloss: rob, clean out (a house, a person)
evidence: Plaut. Aul. 389: numnam ego compīlor miser?
Cic. Par. 6.43: sī sociōs spoliās, aerārium expīlās (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: Istī latrōnēs macellārium omnī argentō ejus spoliāvērunt.
phrases.english: Those robbers robbed the grocer of all his money.

phrases.latin: et strepitust intus. Numnam ego compīlor miser?
phrases.english: and there’s a noise inside. Oh no, am I being robbed?

sources: Lewis & Short: spolio · Lewis & Short: rapio · Lewis & Short: mulco · Lewis & Short: compilo · Lewis & Short: expilo
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 191, 196.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
